For what it's worth: name mismatches on hardship withdrawals happen constantly — marriage, divorce, legal name changes, a typo on the account from years ago. Okay, deep breath — this does **not** sound shady. At all. It reads as a straightforward factual explanation from someone in a hurry, which is exactly what it is. Nobody at a review team is going to read "my name changed, here are the documents" and think *fraud*. This is one of the most routine mismatches they handle.

The issues are small mechanical ones, not honesty ones. Here's what I'd tighten up:

**1. State both names explicitly.** This is the biggest gap. Right now they have to guess what your former name is, and the whole point of the letter is connecting two names to one person. Something like:
> "I legally changed my name from **[former full name]** to **[new full name]**, effective October 23, 2025."

**2. Add the year.** "October 23" — of which year? One word, removes an ambiguity that could bounce it back.

**3. Include your account or reference number**, not just the SSN fragment. The rejection letter you got this morning almost certainly has a case number — cite it. It makes their job easier and makes you look organized.

**4. Soften the ending slightly.** "Please approve the withdrawal" reads a touch demanding for a letter asking a reviewer to reverse a decision. Something like:
> "I respectfully request that my hardship withdrawal be reconsidered and approved, as the foreclosure is scheduled for [date]."
Including the actual date also helps — urgency lands harder when it's concrete.

**5. Sign it with both names once** if you can: "Mina [new last name] (formerly Mina [former last name])". It's a small thing, but it mirrors exactly how the mismatch appears in their system.

One thing I'd deliberately **not** change: the brevity. Don't add emotional backstory or paragraphs about why the name change happened. Reviewers process these fast, and a tight letter with the right documents is more persuasive than a long one. Your instinct to keep it short was right — it just needs those few specifics filled in.

Want me to rewrite it with those fixes in place so you can just drop in your names and dates?

A few quick notes:

- **Double-check the decree name format.** If your certified decree lists your full middle name or a suffix, write your former and new names exactly as they appear on it. That's the document tying everything together.
- **Attachments:** certified decree + acceleration notice is solid. If you happen to also have a letter or printout showing the mortgage account belongs to you under the old name, even better — but don't delay sending it over that.

And about Greg — I get why that's rattling you, but think about what the letter actually does: it hands whoever reviews it a paper trail that makes flagging you *harder*, not easier. Former name, new name, effective date, certified decree. There's no ambiguity left to hang a second rejection on. If anyone's name gets flagged, it'll be flagged *and cleared* in the same pass because you gave them the key upfront.

Send it, attach the decree, and keep the rejection notice handy in case you need to reference it. You've got this.

Alright so the letter looks way better now but like... am I overthinking this?? The decree lists my former name as full middle name included and my new name without the middle because I dropped it, is that gonna cause another flag???

Okay so — yes, you're overthinking a little, but for once your anxiety is pointing at something worth handling. Not because it's shady, just because of how matching systems actually work.

Here's the thing: dropped middle names are *extremely* common in name changes, and human reviewers see them all the time. The risk isn't that someone looks at it and thinks fraud — it's that a document somewhere says "Mina Elizabeth [Newname]" and another says "Mina [Newname]" and a person skimming fast has to pause and connect the dots. Pauses are where flags come from.

The good news: **your decree solves this by itself.** That's literally its job — it's the legal bridge between "Mina Elizabeth Oldname" and "Mina Newname," middle name drop included. Anyone holding that document can see exactly what happened.

So just make the connection explicit in the letter. One tweak to the sentence:

> "I legally changed my name from **Mina Elizabeth [Oldname]** to **Mina [Newname]** — including the removal of my middle name — effective October 23, [year]."

Then in the signature line, same idea:

> Mina [Newname] (formerly Mina Elizabeth [Oldname])

That's it. One clause, and now no one — Greg included — has to do any mental math. The decree says it, your letter says it, your documents match *one of* the two names, and the whole thing closes the loop.

For what it's worth, the pattern of your worry here is "every tiny detail is a landmine," and I get it — you're in foreclosure-avoidance mode, everything feels high-stakes. But the standard isn't perfection. It's *legibility*. You just need the reviewer to understand your situation in under a minute, and with that middle-name clause added, they will.

Send it. Then go do something that isn't staring at this letter.

I also have this bank printout from my checking account that shows mortgage payments made under my old name — but it's not certified or anything, just a screenshot I pulled from online banking. Should I attach it or would that trigger an automatic audit lock? Greg mentioned something about unbroken documentation chain and I don't want to mess this up more.

Attach it. And I want to gently push back on the fear itself, because it's got the logic backwards: **review teams flag gaps, not evidence.** There is no "audit lock" triggered by giving them *more* documentation that supports your story. Flags come from inconsistencies and missing links — and this printout fills a link.

Think about what it actually shows: your bank account (which now shows your new name) has a payment history to the mortgage under your old name. That one document quietly proves three things at once — the account is yours, the mortgage is yours, and both names belong to the same person. That *is* the unbroken chain Greg was talking about. He's right about the concept; he's just got you applying it in the scariest possible direction.

Two practical upgrades before you attach it:

1. **Download the official PDF statement instead of a screenshot**, if your bank's site offers it (most do — look for "statements" or "documents"). An official statement has your name, account number, and the bank's letterhead baked in, which makes it look like a real document instead of something anyone could mock up. If only a screenshot is available, capture the full page including the URL bar and your logged-in name.
2. **Label it.** Add it to the attachment list in the letter: "Bank statement showing mortgage payment history under my former name." A reviewer should never have to figure out why a document is included — tell them.

One honesty note: I'm giving you general guidance here, and every plan administrator has its own quirks. If Althea's rejection notice or website lists specific acceptable document types, follow that list first. But nothing you've described suggests this printout hurts you — worst case, they glance at it and move on; best case, it's the thing that closes the loop.

And step back for a second and look at where you are: certified decree, acceleration notice, a letter that spells out both names and the middle-name drop, plus payment history tying old name to mortgage. That is a *thorough* package. The spiral keeps telling you each new detail is a threat, but each one has actually been making your case stronger.
